GitLab has three different release types:
- Monthly release: A GitLab version (XX.YY.0) published on the 3rd Thursday of every month, containing new features, bug fixes and performance improvements from successful deployments on GitLab.com.
- Patch release: Bug fixes and security updates for maintained versions, published twice monthly.
- Internal release: Private releases for delivering high-severity fixes to GitLab Dedicated within remediation SLAs.

The monthly release is a semver versioned package containing changes from many successful deployments on GitLab.com. Users on GitLab.com, therefore, receive features and bug fixes earlier than users of self-managed installations.

At GitLab, there are two types of patch releases processes:
- Scheduled (default): An SLO-driven patch to publish all available bug and vulnerability fixes per the GitLab maintenance policy. Scheduled twice a month on the Wednesday before and after the monthly release week, planned patches comply with the bug SLO and the security remediation SLAs. The process for proposing a separate database has moved to the required approvals section of our handbook.

Development Required Approvals > Overview > Examples Requiring Approval > Proposing a separate database
As we've learned from our discussions around defining the container registry database schema there are times when it makes sense to separate the data out into its own database. The following sections will describe what data points you should consider and how you would move forward in gaining approval to create a separate database.
Considerations
- Was the feature written in a completely separate code base? Again, using the Container Registry example, this was written in Go and is separate from the main GitLab Rails application.
  - Only do a separate database when it has a completely separate codebase, and that is the only codebase querying the data. For example, Analytics Instrumentation isn't fit for it since the Rails codebase touches it.

Development Required Approvals > Overview > Examples Requiring Approval > Proposing a separate database
Instrumentation isn't fit for it since the Rails codebase touches it.
- Will the feature incur a heavy write load? Writes are harder to scale than reads who can be scaled with replicas.

question: 데이터 분류에서 BLACK 등급 데이터는 어떻게 다뤄야 해?
contexts:
Incident Management > Incident Data Classification
There are four data classification levels defined in GitLab's Data Classification Standard.
- RED data should never be included in incidents, even if the issue is confidential.
- ORANGE and YELLOW data can be included and the Incident Manager managing the incident should ensure the incident issue is marked as confidential or is in an internal note.
The Incident Manager should exercise caution and their best judgement, in general we prefer to use internal notes instead of marking an entire issue confidential if possible. A couple lines of non-descript log data may not represent a data security concern, but a larger set of log, query, or other data must have more restrictive access.

GitLab Data Classification Standard > Standard > Data Classification Levels > ORANGE
its partners, employees, contractors, and customers.
Examples include:
- Personal Data
  - Any vendor who is in possession of any form of Personal Data must have appropriate contractual terms that address GitLab data protection requirements (e.g. a Data Processing Agreement).
  - If Personal Data comprises a part of the data set to be processed, then the data classification for that data set should be Orange and the classification cannot be Yellow or Green, even if the majority of the data set is Yellow or Green data.
  - The source of the Personal Data should not change its classification to a level below Orange since Personal data gathered from public sources is not exempt from protection under certain data protection laws.

Critical Logging Tiering Methodology > Critical Logging Tiering Procedure > Maintaining Critical Logging Tiers > Exceptions
Systems that are exempt from this methodology include any system which carries a data classification of Green. All remaining systems which store or process YELLOW, ORANGE, or RED data are required to have a Critical Logging tier assigned. Data classification will be validated to corroborate that the data stored or processed by the system is truly Green data, per the Data Classification Standard.

Needing separate internal and public facing reviews is not a reason to miss the deadline.

question: 패치 릴리스 기간에는 post-deploy migration(PDM)을 왜 돌리지 않아?
expected: 패치 윈도우 동안 Release Manager는 GitLab.com 배포를 롤백할 수 있어야 하는데, PDM이 프로덕션에서 한 번 실행되면 롤백이 불가능해지기 때문이다. 패치 윈도우는 패치 프로세스 시작부터 패키지 게시까지이며 예약 패치는 보통 목표일 이틀 전에 시작한다.
contexts:
Deployments > Overview and terminology > Post-deploy migration (PDM) execution
start-of-business hours (between approximately 06:00 UTC and 09:00 UTC).
While the standard cadence targets daily execution, PDMs are discretionary and not guaranteed to run every day. Once a PDM has run in production, the deployment can no longer be rolled back, so release managers defer PDMs when they need to keep that option open or when the team's attention is needed elsewhere. PDMs are not run:
- During a patch window, which is the period while a patch release is being prepared, tagged and published.
- During the monthly release window.
- While an incident or change request with the blocks deployments label is active (see Deployment blockers).
- During Production Change Lock periods and for other release management work.

Patch Releases > Patch window
A patch window is the period while a patch release is in progress, from when Release Managers start the patch release process until the packages are published and the final steps are complete. For a scheduled patch this usually starts two days before the target release date, when Release Managers begin deploying security fixes to GitLab.com, and ends on the release date. Exact boundaries vary with each release.
During a patch window, Release Managers keep the ability to roll back GitLab.com deployments. Post-deploy migrations (PDMs) are therefore not run during a patch window, because once a PDM has run in production, the deployment can no longer be rolled back. The same applies to the window around a monthly release.

Deployments > Overview and terminology > Post-deploy migration (PDM) execution
To make GitLab.com packages rollbackable, the post-deploy migrations are independent from the GitLab.com deployment process. These migrations are run in staging and production environments through the post-deploy migration (PDM) pipeline. The PDM is executed manually by release managers as part of standard operational procedures. To minimize the risk of production incidents while ensuring minimal organic traffic, release managers schedule PDM execution during the transition period between APAC end-of-business and EMEA start-of-business hours (between approximately 06:00 UTC and 09:00 UTC).

Deployment Workflow > Post-Deployment Migrations
Post-deployment migrations have their own dedicated workflow and are not guaranteed to run within a specific timeframe. They typically run about once a day, but the deployment team may defer them, for example during a patch window, a monthly release window, or an incident that blocks deployments.
For more details, see the Post-Deploy Migration (PDM) Execution section in the deployments handbook.

Deployments > Overview and terminology > Post-deploy migration (PDM) execution
Production Change Lock periods and for other release management work.
PDMs typically resume at the next suitable execution time after the window ends. In the best case this is late AMER or the start of APAC, so a deferral can mean a delay of a day or more.
To check whether a PDM is pending or has run, see the Delivery: Release information dashboard (internal) and the post-deploy migration pipeline documentation. For questions, contact the Release Managers.
Post deploy migration pipeline
- Source
When a release manager executes the post-deploy migration pipeline:
- Post-deploy migration scripts run on staging
- QA tests execute against staging
- Following a successful QA verification, post-deploy migration scripts run on production.
Details of this pipeline can be found in the post-deploy migration pipeline documentation.
